entities.summary:
**Identity & Significance**: The visual arts have been a cornerstone of human expression since ancient civilizations, with evidence of artistic practices dating back to the Upper Paleolithic period (circa 40,000-10,000 BCE). The practice of creating works primarily visual in nature has evolved over time, influenced by various cultures and forces. From the intricate cave paintings of Lascaux (c. 17,000-15,000 BCE) to the grandiose sculptures of Ancient Greece (c. 8th century-1st century BCE), the visual arts have played a pivotal role in shaping human culture and identity.

**What Happened**: The visual arts have been a dynamic and diverse field, with artists responding to and influencing the world around them. The Renaissance saw a resurgence of classical ideals, while the Impressionist movement (late 19th-early 20th century CE) introduced a new focus on light and color. The 20th century CE witnessed a proliferation of modern and contemporary art movements, including Abstract Expressionism and Pop Art.

**Legacy & Consequence**: The visual arts have had a profound impact on human society, influencing politics, religion, and everyday life. The creation of iconic works such as Leonardo da Vinci's 'Mona Lisa' (c. 1503-1506 CE) and Vincent van Gogh's 'Starry Night' (c. 1889 CE) has left an indelible mark on popular culture. The visual arts continue to shape our understanding of the world and ourselves, inspiring new generations of artists and audiences alike.


The visual arts have also played a significant role in the development of various artistic movements, including the development of photography (invented by Joseph Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 CE) and the rise of digital art (emerging in the 1990s CE). The internet and social media have democratized access to art, allowing artists to showcase their work to a global audience.
